summary: Submission approvable with 1 minor warning(s) — file a corrections record on merge

findings.message: Source redirected to different domain: idp.nature.com
Quote misattributed to Technology Networks; actually said to Medical News Today
findings.details: Article body quotes Corley: "the key point is that this is the first randomized, placebo-controlled clinical evidence that a GLP-1 receptor agonist may slow the biological processes associated with aging in humans," attributed to the cited Technology Networks source. This exact sentence does not appear anywhere in the Technology Networks article (verified against the committed source-3 snapshot, both rendered text and raw HTML). Independent verification (WebSearch + WebFetch of medicalnewstoday.com/articles/glp-1-drugs-ozempic-wegovy-may-slow-biological-aging) confirms Corley made this exact statement to Medical News Today, an outlet not cited anywhere in this submission. The quote itself is real and accurately worded; only the source attribution is wrong. Documented as a corrections-record item rather than grounds for rejection, per editorial policy on wrong-outlet-cited-for-a-real-fact.

content_preview.title: Semaglutide Slows Epigenetic Aging in First Randomized Trial, Nature Communications Study of HIV Patients Finds
content_preview.summary: A UC San Diego-led trial found semaglutide significantly slowed multiple epigenetic aging clocks over 32 weeks in adults with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy, per a Nature Communications study.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 receptor agonist sold as Ozempic and Wegovy, slowed several molecular markers of biological aging in a 32-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial of adults with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy, according to a study published in [Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72861-3) on May 19, 2026. editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (663 words, within the 400-1200 word News range) using the standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know format. Clear headline, accurate summary, logical flow from trial design to results to caveats. No AI self-reference, no promotional language, no defamatory content.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 sources were checked. The chief:review script's local snapshots for source-2 (today.ucsd.edu), source-3 (technologynetworks.com), and source-4 (kpbs.org) contained real article content and were read in full from disk (gunzip + text extraction). Source-0 (nature.com, source-0.html.gz) and source-1 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, source-1.html.gz) returned HTTP 200 but the saved snapshots are bot-block/CAPTCHA challenge pages ('Client Challenge' and 'Checking your browser - reCAPTCHA' respectively) with no article content, despite the manifest recording no error. Per the skill's last-resort clause, I fell back to WebFetch of the live URLs and cross-checked with WebSearch (the WebFetch tool proved unreliable/inconsistent on this specific paper across repeated calls, so all its extractions were corroborated against an independent WebSearch query before being trusted). Verified via WebFetch+WebSearch: PhenoAge -4.9y/year p=0.004, PCGrimAge -3.1y p=0.007, GrimAge V2 -2.3y p=0.009, DunedinPACE -0.09 units (~9%) p=0.01, OMICmAge -2.2y p=0.009 (significant), RetroAge -2.2y p=0.030 (significant), Intrinsic Capacity clock not significant (p=0.31) -- all match the article exactly. Weill Cornell Medicine confirmed as a genuine co-author affiliation (via Alina P. S. Pang). The 'post hoc design, modest sample size, HIV-specific cohort, and 32-week follow-up limit generalizability' quote attributed to Nature Communications was confirmed verbatim via WebSearch indexing of the source text after an initial WebFetch pass gave inconsistent results. Publication date May 19, 2026 confirmed. today.ucsd.edu quotes (2) verified verbatim. kpbs.org quotes (3) verified: 2 verbatim, 1 ('would that snap back?') is a truncation of a longer quoted sentence ('...would that snap back, and then essentially they would be aging at the rate they were,') with the closing comma replaced by a question mark -- meaning is preserved, flagged as a minor style note only, not a correction. technologynetworks.com: the direct quote attributed to this source ('the key point is that this is the first randomized, placebo-controlled clinical evidence...') does NOT appear in the snapshot or the live page; independently confirmed via WebFetch of medicalnewstoday.com that Corley made this exact statement to Medical News Today instead. This is a wrong-outlet misattribution of a real, accurately-worded quote -- filed as a corrections record.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every number, clock name, sample-size figure, and p-value in the article traces to the underlying paper and is independently corroborated by at least one secondary source (UC San Diego Today or Technology Networks). Co-author institution list is accurate. The one factual problem found is not in the data but in sourcing: one direct quote is correctly worded but attributed to the wrong outlet (Technology Networks instead of Medical News Today, which is not among the article's cited sources).
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and measured throughout, consistent with the source material's own cautious framing ('early signal rather than proof'). No sensationalism despite an attention-grabbing topic (Ozempic/longevity).
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/2026-06/ and 2026-07/ for overlapping coverage. No prior Machine Herald article covers this trial or this paper. Two tangentially related prior articles exist (retatrutide weight-loss Phase 3 data; an unrelated ETH Zurich Alzheimer's mechanism study) but neither overlaps in subject or sourcing. A genuinely related piece from 2026-03 on first-in-human epigenetic reprogramming therapy is added as a curated related_articles entry in the meta file.
concerns: One direct quote in the 'What We Know' section is attributed to Technology Networks but was actually said to Medical News Today (not a cited source). The quote itself is accurate; only the outlet attribution is wrong. Filed as a corrections record.
Minor: the KPBS quote 'would that snap back?' truncates a longer sentence and substitutes a question mark for the source's comma. Meaning is unchanged; not filed as a formal correction.

kpbs.org and technologynetworks.com are not yet in config/source_allowlist.txt. Both are legitimate, reputable outlets (KPBS is San Diego's NPR/PBS member station; Technology Networks is an established science trade publication used elsewhere in this beat) -- this is a config gap, not a content problem.
recommendations: Add kpbs.org and technologynetworks.com to config/source_allowlist.txt so future submissions citing them don't re-trigger this warning.
Bot guidance: when pulling a direct quote, verify it appears in the specific URL being cited, not just that the sentiment is attributable to the same speaker across the broader press cycle.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively strong, accurately sourced News piece with one recoverable sourcing error (a real quote attributed to the wrong outlet). APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS: publish with a public corrections record on the misattributed quote.
